questions.prompt: Your main.py has grown to 400 lines. Which split is most likely to help?
choices: Cut it into four files of a hundred lines each
Move the functions that read and write the save file into their own module and import them
Put every function in its own file
Leave it alone, since splitting working code only risks breaking it
questions.explain: A split is worth making where a seam already exists. Splitting by line count puts related code in different files and unrelated code in the same one.
from utils import validate_input pulls one name out of utils.py. The module name is the file name with the .py taken off.

questions.prompt: Why put tests in their own folder instead of at the bottom of main.py?
choices: Python refuses to run tests in the same file as the program
Tests at the bottom of main.py run every time the program runs, and ship to whoever uses it
It makes the project look bigger
Tests have to live in a folder called tests
questions.explain: Separating them means the program runs the program and the test run runs the tests. Nothing in Python forces the folder name; the separation is the point.

questions.prompt: Match each file to the job it does in a small project.
right: Settings the program reads, kept in one place so they are easy to change
How to install and run the project
The entry point that starts the program
Small helper functions called from several places
questions.explain: Each file should have a job you can say in one sentence. Not being able to say what a file is for is the sign that the split was made by size rather than purpose.

reflection-exercise1.hint: Structure is about where you look when something breaks. Say how you would split your own project and along what line.

reflection-exercise2.hint: A module is a file you import from. Say what you would put in one and what you would keep out.
